script.opening: “Hello, doctor. I want to go back to work now — I’ve been off four months and I feel much better. But I have a meeting with HR next week and I don’t know if I should tell them I have MS. If they hear ‘MS’ they will think I’m disabled and they’ll find a way to get rid of me.”

facts.text: “I’m a housekeeper in a big hotel — three years there. Stripping beds, carrying linen bags, pushing the trolley, and two days a week in the laundry room. It’s very hot in there.”

facts.topic: How she is now (if asked about symptoms)
facts.text: “Much better. By the afternoon I’m tired — really tired, not normal tired. When I’m tired my right foot drags a bit.” If asked about heat: “In a hot bath my legs go heavy, then it goes when I cool down.”

No problems with eyesight now, no double vision, no new numbness, no falls since the hospital. Bladder (only if asked directly): “Sometimes I have to rush to the toilet — I make it, but only just.” Bowels fine. Leg pains at night are better on pregabalin.

facts.topic: Relapse check (if asked about new symptoms in the last few weeks)
facts.text: “No, nothing new. It’s been steady for two months.”
“I take them all — my husband reminds me. The MS nurse does my blood tests.” Not had the flu jab this year: “Nobody said.”
“I was very low after the hospital. Now — worried, not sad. I sleep OK.” No thoughts of self-harm.

facts.topic: Driving (only if asked whether she drives or how she gets to work)
facts.text: “I drive. The shift starts at six, there’s no bus.” If asked whether the DVLA knows: hesitate, then “No… I didn’t tell them. If they take my licence, I lose my job anyway.” If asked about the right leg when driving: “It’s my right foot that drags when I’m tired. Driving home after a shift — I’m careful.”

facts.topic: Colleagues (hidden, say if asked what people at work know)
facts.text: “I told my supervisor it was my back. I didn’t want everyone talking.” Ask: “Do I have to tell my colleagues?”

Lives with husband Tomasz (warehouse supervisor, works days) and daughter Zofia, 9. Moved from Poland 12 years ago; English is good. Does not smoke, drinks rarely, no drugs. Money is tight on statutory sick pay.

Be anxious and a little guarded. Mention the driving only if asked whether you drive or how you get to work; mention telling colleagues “it was my back” only if asked what people know. If the doctor explains the Equality Act clearly, become relieved. If the doctor lectures you about the DVLA or threatens to report you, become defensive (“So I lose my job then?”). If the doctor explains calmly that most people with MS keep their licence and the DVLA must decide, agree to tell them this week. Ask: “Is MS a disability?” and “Do I have to tell my colleagues?”

ice.ideas: “If I say MS, they will see me as disabled and weak.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she has not told the DVLA and is frightened that losing her licence means losing the job (no bus at 6 am); she has told colleagues it was a back injury. Underneath is fear of being pushed out and of money running out.
ice.expectations: Advice on what to say to HR, and a fit note so she can go back.

cues: “They’ll find a way to get rid of me.” — fear of discrimination and of losing income.
“By the afternoon I’m really tired, and my foot drags.” — residual function that matters for duties and for driving.
“The shift starts at six, there’s no bus.” — she drives, and the DVLA has not been told.

checkpoints.text: Assesses current function in relation to the job: fatigue pattern, right-leg drag, heat sensitivity, bladder urgency, pain, mood — and confirms no new symptoms suggesting relapse
Explores the job demands (lifting, hot laundry, early shift) and asks how she gets to work — discovering she drives and has not told the DVLA

Explains that MS is a disability under the Equality Act 2010 from the point of diagnosis: protection from discrimination and a duty on the employer to consider reasonable adjustments; disclosure is her choice, and colleagues need not be told

Offers a fit note marked “may be fit for work” with specific phased return, amended duties (no heavy lifting, avoid the laundry heat), altered hours and rest breaks; suggests Occupational Health and Access to Work
Explains the legal duty to tell the DVLA about MS, that the DVLA decides and most people keep their licence, and advises not to drive when her leg is weak or she is very tired until assessed
Offers the flu vaccine, signposts the MS nurse, and safety-nets for relapse (new weakness, visual loss, numbness, balance) and bladder symptoms
Responds to her fear of being “labelled” with empathy and accurate reassurance; avoids a lecture on driving and treats her as a partner in the decisions

worked.lbl: Explore the job, not just the illness
worked.txt: “Talk me through a normal shift — what does your body have to do, and how do you get there for six?”

“MS is one of the conditions the Equality Act counts as a disability from the day it is diagnosed. That’s a protection, not a label: your employer must not treat you worse because of it, and must look at reasonable changes to help you work.”
“Whether you tell HR is your choice. If they don’t know, it is harder for them to make adjustments. Your colleagues don’t need to know anything unless you want them to.”

“There is one thing the law does require: anyone diagnosed with MS has to tell the DVLA. Most people with MS keep their licence — the DVLA decide, sometimes with a short-term licence. Until they do, please don’t drive when your right leg is weak or you are exhausted.”
“I can write a fit note saying you may be fit for work with changes — a phased return over four weeks, no heavy lifting, no laundry shifts for now, and rest breaks. That gives HR something concrete.”

f.learning: Return-to-work consultations test whether the doctor can turn medical facts into practical, lawful advice. MS (like cancer and HIV) is deemed a disability under the Equality Act 2010 from diagnosis, so the employer must not discriminate and must consider reasonable adjustments — disclosure is voluntary but usually helps. The fit note (“may be fit for work”) is a powerful tool: be specific about phased return, amended duties, altered hours and workplace adaptations. Occupational Health and the Access to Work scheme add support. Always ask about driving in neurological conditions: anyone with MS must tell the DVLA, which then decides; the GP explains the duty and records the advice, and GMC guidance describes when a doctor may need to inform the DVLA if a patient continues to drive when unfit. Heat-related worsening (Uhthoff phenomenon) and fatigue are common and should shape adjustments. Offer the annual flu vaccine (infection can trigger relapse) and keep the MS nurse involved.

knowledge.guideline: Equality Act 2010 (Schedule 1: MS deemed a disability from diagnosis) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current edition, 2025) · DWP Getting the most out of the fit note: guidance for healthcare professionals (2024) · NICE NG220 Multiple sclerosis in adults: management (2022) · GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA (2017) · UKHSA Green Book chapter 19: influenza (2025)
knowledge.summary: Assess function against the job, explain Equality Act protection and reasonable adjustments, write a specific “may be fit” fit note, find the undeclared driving and explain the DVLA duty calmly.

points.t: MS, cancer and HIV are deemed disabilities from diagnosis, regardless of current severity. Employers must not discriminate and have a duty to make reasonable adjustments. Disclosure is voluntary, but an employer cannot be expected to adjust for what it does not know.

“May be fit for work” with options: phased return, altered hours, amended duties, workplace adaptations. Be specific and time-limited (for example 4–6 weeks). If the employer cannot accommodate, the note counts as “not fit” — she is not penalised.
Occupational Health (via the employer) assesses and recommends adjustments. Access to Work (DWP) can fund support, equipment or travel costs, including taxis when public transport is not usable.

A car driver with MS must tell the DVLA (online or form CN1). The DVLA may issue a full or short-period licence or ask for information. Advise not to drive if symptoms affect control (for example right-leg weakness or severe fatigue). Not telling the DVLA can lead to a fine and invalidate insurance.

Fatigue (pacing, rest breaks, amantadine), heat sensitivity (Uhthoff phenomenon — temporary worsening with heat, not a relapse), bladder urgency (toilet access; consider bladder review), neuropathic pain, mood. A relapse is new or worse symptoms lasting more than 24 hours without fever or infection.

Dimethyl fumarate needs lymphocyte and LFT monitoring by the MS team (risk of PML with prolonged lymphopenia). Offer the annual influenza vaccine — MS is a chronic neurological condition in the at-risk group, and infection can trigger relapse.
Pass candidates answer the HR question well. Clear pass candidates also find the driving, handle it without threat, and leave her with a fit note she can hand to HR.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Nowak? It’s Dr Lewis. Can I just check your date of birth, and that you’re somewhere you can talk?
model.why: Identity and privacy on the telephone

model.text: Yes, I’m at home. I want to go back to work but I don’t know if I should tell them about the MS. They’ll think I’m disabled and get rid of me.
That sounds like a real worry. Let’s make sure you leave with a plan for that meeting. First, how are you physically now?
model.why: Acknowledges the fear and signposts the structure

model.text: Better. By the afternoon I’m very tired and my right foot drags a bit. Heat makes my legs heavy.
Anything new in the last few weeks — eyesight, numbness, balance, falls? And any problems with your bladder or bowels?
model.why: Relapse screen plus bladder symptoms that affect work

model.text: Nothing new. Sometimes I have to rush to the toilet.
Tell me about the job — what does a shift involve, and how do you get there for six?
model.why: Job demands and the route to the driving question

model.text: Beds, linen bags, the hot laundry two days a week. I drive — there’s no bus that early.
Thank you. Have you had a chance to let the DVLA know about the MS?
No… if they take my licence I lose the job anyway.

I understand why that’s frightening. The law says anyone diagnosed with MS needs to tell the DVLA — but most people keep their licence. They may want a report from your neurologist. Until they decide, please don’t drive when your leg is weak or you’re exhausted. If transport becomes a problem, Access to Work can sometimes pay towards taxis.
model.why: Legal duty explained calmly, interim safety advice, practical help

model.text: OK. And is MS a disability? I don’t want them to see me like that.

Under the Equality Act, yes — from the day it’s diagnosed. That protects you: they mustn’t treat you worse because of it, and they must look at reasonable changes. Whether you tell HR is your choice, but it lets them help. Your colleagues don’t need to know unless you want them to.
model.why: Accurate law framed as protection; answers both questions

model.text: I’ll do a fit note saying you may be fit for work with changes: a phased return over four weeks, no heavy lifting, no laundry room for now, and rest breaks. HR may ask Occupational Health to see you — that’s normal and helpful.
model.why: Specific fit note and Occupational Health

model.text: Two more things: you’re due a flu jab — infections can trigger relapses — and please call your MS nurse or us if anything new comes on for more than a day, like weakness, blurred vision or numbness. What will you say to HR, and what will you do about the DVLA?
I’ll take the fit note and tell them it’s MS. I’ll fill in the DVLA form this week and not drive when my leg is bad.

social.t: Physically demanding, early-shift job; household finances strained on statutory sick pay. Practical solutions (phased return, Access to Work travel costs) matter more than reassurance alone.
A worker who has built a life in the UK may fear that illness threatens her job security; make sure she knows her employment rights apply fully.

legal.t: Deemed disability from diagnosis; reasonable adjustments duty; protection from discrimination and dismissal because of disability.

Legal duty on the licence holder to tell the DVLA. The doctor advises and documents; GMC guidance sets out when a doctor should inform the DVLA if a patient continues to drive when unfit and will not tell them.

professional.t: A vague “may be fit” is unhelpful. Name the adjustments and the duration so the employer can act.

community.t: MS specialist nurse; MS Society and MS Trust work and driving guides; Access to Work; ACAS advice on reasonable adjustments; Citizens Advice for employment rights.

redFlags: New neurological symptoms lasting over 24 hours (relapse)
Bladder retention or incontinence; infection symptoms
psychosocial: Job demands: lifting, heat, early shifts
How she travels to work — driving
ice: Idea: MS means being seen as disabled
Concern: losing the job; hidden fear about the licence
Expectation: advice for HR and a fit note

playbook.diagnosis: Relapsing-remitting MS in remission after a recent relapse, with residual fatigue, mild right-leg weakness, heat sensitivity and urinary urgency; ready for a supported return to work; undeclared to the DVLA.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your MS is settled at the moment, but tiredness, heat and your right leg still need some changes at work — and the DVLA needs to know about the diagnosis.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried that saying ‘MS’ will cost you your job. The law is actually on your side — and telling them is what lets them make changes for you.”
management.psychosocial: Phased return protects income and health; Access to Work for travel; husband’s support with transport on bad days.
sharedPlan: Fit note: may be fit for work — phased return over 4 weeks, no heavy lifting, no laundry room, rest breaks
Occupational Health via employer; Access to Work
Tell the DVLA this week; do not drive when the leg is weak or very tired
Flu vaccine; continue DMF monitoring with the MS team
Consider bladder review if urgency persists
safetyNet: New weakness, visual loss, numbness or balance problems lasting more than 24 hours — MS nurse or GP same day; 111 out of hours
Fever with worsening symptoms — infection can mimic relapse
Review after the HR meeting or before the fit note ends

pitfalls.intro: This looks like a quick advice call about HR. It is failed by candidates who never ask about driving, or who answer with vague reassurance and no usable fit note.

items.fail: Never asks how she gets to work or whether she drives.
items.why: MS carries a legal duty to tell the DVLA, and her right leg drags when tired — a safety issue for her and others.
items.fix: Ask about the commute and driving as part of the job history.

items.fail: Tells her she “must” tell HR, or that she should keep it quiet.
items.why: Disclosure is her choice; both extremes ignore the law and her autonomy.
items.fix: Explain the Equality Act protection and the practical benefit of disclosure, then let her decide.

items.fail: Responds to the DVLA admission with a warning about reporting her.
items.why: Threats make her defensive and less likely to act; most people with MS keep their licence.
items.fix: Explain the duty calmly, give interim advice, and offer practical help with transport.

timeMap.d: Identity, privacy; hear the worry about being “labelled”.
Fatigue, leg, heat, bladder, mood; relapse screen; the job; how she gets there — driving.
DVLA duty calmly; Equality Act; disclosure choice; specific fit note; Occupational Health; Access to Work.
Flu vaccine, MS nurse, relapse safety-net, teach-back.

wordPics.clearFail: Gives generic reassurance (“they can’t sack you”), no assessment of function, no fit note, driving never mentioned or handled with a threat.
wordPics.fail: Answers the HR question correctly but misses the driving, or finds it and gives inaccurate advice (“you must stop driving now” or “you don’t need to tell them”); the fit note is vague.
wordPics.pass: Assesses function against the job, explains the Equality Act and reasonable adjustments, offers a specific “may be fit” fit note, finds the driving and explains the DVLA duty, and safety-nets for relapse.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, done warmly and efficiently: frames disability status as protection, answers the colleagues question, handles the DVLA calmly with interim advice and Access to Work for transport, adds the flu vaccine and MS nurse, and confirms her plan by teach-back.

avoid.dont: “If you keep driving I’ll have to tell the DVLA myself.”
avoid.instead: “The law asks you to tell them — most people with MS keep their licence. Can we agree you’ll do it this week?”
avoid.why: Starting with a threat damages trust; the GMC route is a last resort.

avoid.instead: “The Equality Act protects you and means they must look at reasonable changes.”
avoid.why: Accurate law reassures better than a blanket promise.

avoid.instead: “I’ll write a phased return over four weeks, no heavy lifting, no laundry shifts and rest breaks.”
avoid.why: A specific fit note is usable; a vague one is not.
